principle.name: Follow Go Idioms
principle.description: Always use idiomatic Go patterns and conventions. Go has a strong culture of simplicity and clarity. Avoid patterns from other languages that don't fit Go's design.
principle.rationale: Idiomatic Go code is more readable, maintainable, and performs better. The Go community values simple, clear solutions over clever abstractions.

example.good: Always check errors immediately and handle or return them
example.bad: Ignore errors or use try-catch style patterns

principle.name: Interface Design
principle.description: Design small, focused interfaces that define behavior, not data. Interfaces should be accepted as parameters and structs should be returned.
principle.rationale: Small interfaces are easier to implement and test. They promote loose coupling and make code more flexible and testable.

principle.name: Package Organization
principle.description: Organize packages by their responsibility, not by layer. Each package should have a single, well-defined purpose. Avoid circular dependencies between packages.
principle.rationale: Clear package boundaries make code easier to navigate, understand, and maintain. They also prevent import cycles which are not allowed in Go.

examples.good: - Package names: lowercase, single word, descriptive - Exported names: PascalCase (e.g., HttpClient) - Unexported names: camelCase (e.g., httpClient) - Interface names: usually -er suffix (e.g., Reader, Writer) - Constants: PascalCase or UPPER_CASE
examples.bad: - Package names: mixedCase or underscores - Inconsistent capitalization - Abbreviations without context

guidelines.guideline: Always provide a way to stop goroutines
Use sync.WaitGroup to wait for completion
Close channels from the producer side only
Use range over channels for consumers

pitfall.why_problematic: Ignoring errors leads to silent failures and makes debugging difficult. Go's explicit error handling is a feature, not a bug.
pitfall.correct_approach: Always handle errors by either returning them (with context), logging them, or explicitly ignoring them with a comment explaining why.

pitfall.why_problematic: Spawning too many goroutines can exhaust memory and degrade performance. Concurrency adds complexity that should be justified by real benefits.
pitfall.correct_approach: Use goroutines when you have actual concurrent work to do. Consider worker pools with bounded concurrency for managing many tasks.

pitfall.why_problematic: Go does not allow import cycles. Circular dependencies indicate poor package organization and make code difficult to understand.
pitfall.correct_approach: Refactor to eliminate cycles by: - Moving shared code to a new package - Using interfaces to break dependencies - Reorganizing package responsibilities

pitfall.why_problematic: Global mutable state makes code hard to test, reason about, and can cause race conditions in concurrent code.
pitfall.correct_approach: Pass dependencies explicitly through function parameters or struct fields. Use dependency injection patterns for better testability.
